This paper introduces a novel approach to the containment problem for extended regular expressions, enhancing basic regex capabilities with intersection and complementation while handling infinite alphabets via potentially limitless character sets. Unlike traditional methods that fail to manage extended operators or such vast character collections, the proposed algorithm eliminates the necessity of converting expressions to equivalent automata. We propose a concept termed multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics designed to significantly lower the count of focal plane imators required for wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) technology. In the proposed MuLE setup, a single LE mirror is partitioned into distinct segments, each directing reflected X-rays to converge onto one common image sensor within a multiplexed arrangement. When these LE segments are set at varying rotation angles, a point source is reconstructed into an orientation-dependent cross image by the LE optics; identifying the image's rotation thus reveals which specific segment focused the X-rays onto that sensor. This study examines how velocities influence the dark matter halo mass function (DMF), a key issue within the $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model. Although linear theory predicts that velocity effects are primarily a perturbation valid at large scales, nonlinear dynamics can generate significant deviations on smaller lengths. Utilizing synthetic data produced by $N$-body simulations, we applied a deep neural network—specifically a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)—to train the model in predicting dark matter halo masses across a wide spectrum of 27 dimensional coordinates, which combine density and velocity fields for seven distinct $N$=27 components at each of $N$=27 nodes in $d$=3 (or similar). Our results show that deep learning models can effectively recover the impact of velocities even when trained solely on linearly evolved data, although the efficiency of these predictions increases with the level of nonlinear growth. Furthermore, by comparing predictions based on linear data against those using data already nonlinear in a $\Lambda$CDM framework, we find that velocity-field effects are amplified by cosmic structure formation. Finally, by analyzing the predicted deviations caused by velocities against those derived from perturbed theories, we uncover scenarios where non-linear velocity terms become prominent, offering new insights into the need for nonlinear corrections.
